subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove that sin A sin(π/3 + A) sin(π/3 − A) = (1/4) sin 3A.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 8 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS, Very Short Answer question 39(i), book p.92. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The two marks sit on the difference-of-squares step and on recognising sin 3A; grouping the last two factors stays on the page as unmarked working. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1-Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, and Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations holds two of those ten slots. NUMERIC CHECK before authoring: both sides were evaluated at A = 0.3, 0.7, 1.1 and 37°; they agreed to 12 decimal places at every value. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each move in order.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Group the last two factors
steps.margin_note: Write sin A outside a bracket and keep the matched pair inside it. The pair is the part that simplifies.
lines: L.H.S = sin A · [sin(π/3 + A) sin(π/3 − A)]
sin(X + Y) sin(X − Y) = sin²X − sin²Y

recall.must_convey: That the last two factors are grouped as a sum times a difference, ready for sin²X − sin²Y.
accept: keep sin a outside and bracket the other two
the second and third factors are a sum and a difference of the same angles
sin x plus y into sin x minus y is sin squared x minus sin squared y
rendu factors ni bracket lo pettali

steps.why: The second and third factors are a sum and a difference of the same two angles, so they multiply to a difference of squares. sin A is left outside for now.
common_mistakes: Expanding sin(π/3 + A) and sin(π/3 − A) term by term.
Grouping sin A with one of the other factors.
steps.memory_tip: A sum times a difference of the same two angles is a difference of squares.

steps.label: Apply sin(X+Y) sin(X−Y)
steps.margin_note: First mark. X is π/3 and Y is A, so the bracket becomes 3/4 − sin²A. Keep sin A multiplying it.
lines: With X = π/3 and Y = A:

recall.must_convey: That with X = π/3 and Y = A the bracket becomes sin²(π/3) − sin²A = 3/4 − sin²A.
accept: x is pi by three and y is a so it is sin squared pi by three minus sin squared a
sin pi by three squared is three by four
the bracket becomes three by four minus sin squared a
sin pi by three square ante three by four
apply the difference of squares formula
reject: sin three a is three sin a minus four sin cubed a

steps.why: sin(π/3) = √3/2, so its square is 3/4. That 3/4 is what later supplies the 3 in 3 sin A − 4 sin³A.
common_mistakes: Writing the result as sin²A − 3/4, with the terms the wrong way round.

steps.label: Recognise sin 3A
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Multiply sin A in, then take 1/4 out of both terms. What is left is the standard expansion of sin 3A.

recall.must_convey: That sin A (3/4 − sin²A) = (1/4)(3 sin A − 4 sin³A) = (1/4) sin 3A.
accept: multiply sin a in and take one by four out
three sin a minus four sin cubed a is sin three a
so the left side is a quarter of sin three a
one by four bayaki teeste sin three a vasthundi
the answer is one by four sin three a
reject: apply the difference of squares formula

steps.why: Multiplying sin A into the bracket gives (3/4)sin A − sin³A. Taking 1/4 out leaves 3 sin A − 4 sin³A, which is exactly sin 3A.
common_mistakes: Taking 1/4 out of only the first term.
Writing sin 3A as 4 sin³A − 3 sin A, which is the cosine pattern.
steps.memory_tip: sin 3A = 3 sin A − 4 sin³A: sine starts with 3, cosine starts with 4.
